name: ChaChaCha
baseline: OpenSSL ChaCha20/ChaCha20-Poly1305 (assembly and EVP), BoringSSL stitched AVX2 ChaCha20-Poly1305
workload: ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD seal/open at protocol-realistic sizes (QUIC 1200-1350B, WireGuard 1360-1420B, 4KB TLS record, 9000B jumbo, 16384B TLS 1.3 max record, 32-64KiB bulk) measured in core cycles/byte via perf_event_open, pinned to one core, best-of-7 internal reps x best-of-3 runs, on AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
claimed_speedup: AEAD seal vs OpenSSL: +19.3% to +47.6% across sizes on Zen5 (e.g. +45.4% at WireGuard 1360-1420B, +22.4% at 16384B); vs BoringSSL: +49.4% to +57.4%; vs Intel IPsec-MB: +3.8% to +19.9%. Raw AVX-512 ChaCha20 vs OpenSSL: +25-33% on Zen5, +5-8% on Zen4 for >=4KB streams. Raw AVX2 ChaCha20 vs OpenSSL and BoringSSL: +10% Zen5, +7-8% Zen4 for messages above a few KB
hardware: AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5, Turin) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512 only (no portable/scalar-only fallback path shown as competitive); OpenSSL is measured both as raw vendored assembly (openssl-asm) and via EVP (openssl-evp) which carries provider dispatch overhead, so the EVP-vs-EVP comparison would show an even larger margin than the asm-vs-asm numbers quoted; BoringSSL comparison for AVX-512 is AEAD-only since BoringSSL has no AVX-512 ChaCha20 raw kernel; single author, very new/unreviewed project
caveats: Single-author project with only 1 GitHub star and no independent review; author explicitly documents methodology carefully (per-call fixed-overhead table) and shows all four implementations round-trip-checked for correctness, which is unusually rigorous for a solo project, but numbers have not been reproduced by anyone else
found_via: GitHub: gh search code 'handshakes per second' "faster" (surfaced via a broader ChaCha20 AVX-512/TLS-record code search, then opened repo README and result.md directly)

name: curve25519 (mehdi sotoodeh / "Mehdi")
baseline: OpenSSL Ed25519 (EVP_PKEY_ED25519 via the EVP API), OpenSSL 1.1.1
workload: Ed25519 key-pair creation, public-key derivation, X25519 shared-secret computation, and Ed25519 message signing, timed in CPU cycles via TSC read, comparing this library's hand-written x86-64 assembly implementation ('make asm && make openssl') against OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY_ED25519 API for the same operations
claimed_speedup: On HP EliteBook 755 G5 (Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1): CreateKeyPair 64.50% faster (74,822 vs 210,738 cycles), CreateSharedKey 38.81% faster (270,930 vs 442,750 cycles), SignMessage 81.53% faster (78,628 vs 425,656 cycles); but CalculatePublicKey is 51.45% SLOWER than OpenSSL (316,096 vs 208,714 cycles). Separately, standalone X25519 base-point scalar multiplication is claimed 6.2x-19.5x faster than Google's curve25519-donna (not OpenSSL) across several platforms/compilers, fastest at 43,229 cycles on an Intel Core i7-2670QM
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ via 'make asm' (hand-written x86-64 assembly kernels, not affected by the portable-C build's missing -O level); portable-C fallback build uses CFLAGS=-DNDEBUG -m64 -Wno-format with no explicit -O2/-O3 (Release build sets only -DNDEBUG per Rules.mk), but this does not affect the asm path that is actually benchmarked against OpenSSL
hardware: HP EliteBook 755 G5, x86_64 (OpenSSL comparison); Intel Core i7-2670QM (internal cycle-count tables); exact CPU model for the OpenSSL comparison run not given beyond laptop model
tradeoffs: One of four benchmarked operations (CalculatePublicKey) is markedly slower than OpenSSL, so the library is not a strict win across the board; portable-C build has no stated optimization level (only the asm build is used for the OpenSSL comparison); constant-time/blinding variants are slower than the non-hardened V1.1 numbers; abandoned since 2020, predates OpenSSL 3.x and modern OpenSSL X25519/Ed25519 assembly optimizations, so the OpenSSL side of the comparison is likely stale
caveats: Benchmark is from 2015-2019 era against OpenSSL 1.1.1 on a single laptop; OpenSSL has significantly optimized its X25519/Ed25519 assembly since 1.1.1, so the margin may have shrunk or reversed on current OpenSSL; the curve25519-donna comparison (6.2x-19.5x) is a different, non-KNOWN_LIST baseline and mixes results across different compilers/platforms rather than one apples-to-apples run
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "X25519" "faster than" (surfaced msotoodeh/curve25519 README mention, then opened repo, Makefile, Rules.mk and test/openssl_test.c directly)

name: ztls
workload: Sans-I/O TLS 1.3 in-memory application-data round trips (client-to-server, server-to-client, ping-pong) at record sizes 16B, 128B, 1350B, 8192B, 16384B, across TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, over caller-owned in-memory transport (no sockets), n=10 captures with formal confidence intervals
claimed_speedup: Headline row (AES-128-GCM ping-pong, 1350B records, x86_64 c7i.2xlarge): ztls 790.7 ns/op vs rustls 1447.5 ns/op (1.83x slower than ztls) vs OpenSSL libssl 1820.5 ns/op (2.30x slower than ztls); ztls executes 42.7% of libssl's cycles/op and 54.8% of rustls's on that row. Beats libssl on every comparable app-data row on both x86_64 and aarch64; beats rustls on all AES-GCM rows (smallest win +65%) but loses to rustls on small ChaCha20-Poly1305 records on x86_64 (16B/128B: -50% to -56%, honestly disclosed)
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2, ReleaseFast (captured before ztls required Zig 0.16; author notes relative deltas stand, absolute numbers are historical); OpenSSL 3.6.3 and rustls 0.23.4x as comparison backends
hardware: AWS c7i.2xlarge (Intel Xeon, x86_64) and c7g.2xlarge (Graviton4, aarch64); third platform is Apple M1 Max (macOS)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha, API not stable; TLS 1.3 only (no 1.2 fallback, no DTLS, no Windows); crypto primitives (AEAD, ECDHE, signatures, SHA-2) are still delegated to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL, AWS-LC, or BoringSSL) which allocates during setup, so the zero-allocation claim covers only ztls's own framing/parsing/transcript code, not the crypto backend; loses to rustls on small ChaCha20-Poly1305 records on x86_64; full-handshake row is explicitly documented as non-equivalent across implementations (different certificate-verification scope) and the project itself says not to quote it as a comparison
caveats: Extremely new/pre-alpha project (7 stars, last push same day as this search) from a single named author; despite that, the project's own documentation is unusually rigorous about measurement validity (explicit per-row equivalence table, disclosed losses, non-equivalent rows called out and excluded, regression gate against a committed n=10 baseline) which is why it clears tier A despite low adoption; numbers are the project's own captures, not yet independently reproduced by a third party
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "handshakes per second" "faster" surfaced mattrobenolt/ztls README and docs/research/PERFORMANCE.md and PRODUCTION_READINESS.md, opened directly
